newsitem.title: CANADA: Peru, Japan prepare for summit on Lima hostages.
newsitem.headline: Peru, Japan prepare for summit on Lima hostages.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto flew to Canada on Friday for a summit with Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori amid signs of Tokyo's unease about Lima's increasingly tough stance toward the 45-day-old hostage crisis.
The leaders arrived separately at Toronto's international airport in light snow and went directly to a downtown hotel to prepare for the Saturday morning meeting.
The summit was hastily arranged as a rift appeared to widen between Lima and Tokyo on negotiations with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru.

Hashimoto said the crisis had reached a "delicate stage," an indication he wants a quick resolution. But the Peruvian leader said he was prepared to wait for months, even raising the specter of the U.S. Embassy crisis in Iran 17 years ago.

"I don't have the faintest idea how long it will be before there is a solution to the crisis. Remember that there was a seizure in Iran that lasted 444 days," Fujimori told Argentina's Clarin newspaper in an interview published after his departure for Canada.
"We are not going to give in to the terrorists' demands. As time goes by, offers made by the government are being progressively reduced," he said.
Hashimoto declared before leaving Tokyo that "there must be no caving in to terrorism" at the summit.
But a Japanese government source said Hashimoto planned to urge Fujimori to soften his position and allow the rebels' main demand onto the agenda for negotiations.
The source said Tokyo and Lima were divided over whether to give ground on the rebels' insistence that Peru free 400 of their comrades from Peruvian jails.
Talks with the estimated 15 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holding the hostages have been deadlocked for weeks over Fujimori's refusal to discuss the demand.

The MRTA's international spokesman warned that Fujimori was playing a dangerous game by suggesting he could wait weeks or even months rather than accept the rebel demands about freeing the jailed guerrillas.
The spokesman, Isaac Velazco, urged Hashimoto to convince Fujimori to seek a political solution to the crisis.
"The Japanese government will be responsible as well if this is not resolved (peacefully) because it is backing Fujimori's moves," Velazco said.

Japan's concern deepened this week after provocative action by Peruvian police outside the compound, where two dozen Japanese businessman and diplomats are among the captives held by rebels since Dec. 17.

Since last Friday, police have stepped up the war of nerves, saying they wanted to wear down the rebels' resistance. They sent convoys rumbling past the residence, blasted martial music and buzzed the residence with helicopters and planes.
The Japanese and Peruvian leaders agreed to meet two days ago after Hashimoto urged Fujimori to exercise caution to avoid "accidents or incidents."
The two, who have met twice in the past four months, chose Canada because they wanted to meet on neutral ground at a convenient mid-point.
Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, was accompanied by two cabinet ministers, five congressmen and his son Kenjy.

Fujimori was met by Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent, one of more than 500 original hostages seized in the guerrilla raid during a reception in honor of the Japanese emperor. Vincent, a veteran diplomat, later became one of the key mediators between the rebels and the government.

"Canada is able to provide a positive constructive environment," Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy said in explaining Ottawa's role. "We don't bring any of our own agendas. We've been very supportive of the negotiating process."
